items.readable_text:
Content:
Previously, we learned how to construct a linear relationship between two variables. Now, we'll explore how to express such relationships using function notation.

Content:
For example, suppose the height [MATH: H] of a tree, in centimeters, [MATH: t] months after planting it is given by the linear equation

Content:
[MATH: H = 120 + 3t.]

Content:
According to this linear model,

Content:
- the tree was [MATH: 120\,\textrm{cm}] high when it was planted, and
- the tree grows by [MATH: 3\,\textrm{cm}] each month.

Content:
In practice, we tend to model linear relationships of this kind using function notation, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: H(t) = 120 + 3t]

Content:
This gives us the following additional information:

Content:
- The height [MATH: H] of the tree depends on the time [MATH: t] since the tree was planted. For this reason, we call [MATH: H] the dependent variable, and [MATH: t] the independent variable.
- Writing [MATH: H(t)] makes it clear that the height of the tree depends on the time and not vice versa.

Content:
We can use our function to make predictions about the tree's height. For example, to find the height of the tree after [MATH: 36] months, we substitute [MATH: t = 36] into the height function:

Content:
[MATH: H(36)|= 120 + 3(36); = 120 + 108; = 228.]

Content:
Thus, the tree will be [MATH: 228] centimeters tall after [MATH: 36] months.

sections.normalized_html:
The temperature [MATH: T] of a liquid, in degrees Fahrenheit, [MATH: t] minutes after it starts cooling is given by

[MATH: T(t) = 80 - 1.75t.] What will the temperature be after [MATH: 24] minutes?
sections.readable_text:
The temperature [MATH: T] of a liquid, in degrees Fahrenheit, [MATH: t] minutes after it starts cooling is given by

[MATH: T(t) = 80 - 1.75t.]
What will the temperature be after [MATH: 24] minutes?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We are told that the temperature is given by the function

[MATH: T(t) = 80 - 1.75t,] where [MATH: t] represents the number of minutes after cooling starts.

We substitute [MATH: t = 24] into the temperature function:

[MATH: T(24)|= 80 − 1.75(24); = 80 − 42; = 38.]

Thus, the temperature will be [MATH: 38^\circ\mathrm{F}] after [MATH: 24] minutes.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Previously, we learned how to construct a linear relationship between two variables. Now, we'll explore how to express such relationships using function notation.

Content:
For example, suppose the height [MATH: H] of a tree, in centimeters, [MATH: t] months after planting it is given by the linear equation

Content:
[MATH: H = 120 + 3t.]

Content:
According to this linear model,

Content:
- the tree was [MATH: 120\,\textrm{cm}] high when it was planted, and
- the tree grows by [MATH: 3\,\textrm{cm}] each month.

Content:
In practice, we tend to model linear relationships of this kind using function notation, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: H(t) = 120 + 3t]

Content:
This gives us the following additional information:

Content:
- The height [MATH: H] of the tree depends on the time [MATH: t] since the tree was planted. For this reason, we call [MATH: H] the dependent variable, and [MATH: t] the independent variable.
- Writing [MATH: H(t)] makes it clear that the height of the tree depends on the time and not vice versa.

Content:
We can use our function to make predictions about the tree's height. For example, to find the height of the tree after [MATH: 36] months, we substitute [MATH: t = 36] into the height function:

Content:
[MATH: H(36)|= 120 + 3(36); = 120 + 108; = 228.]

Content:
Thus, the tree will be [MATH: 228] centimeters tall after [MATH: 36] months.

---

Item 2 — Example: Evaluating a Linear Function Model

Example Prompt:
The temperature [MATH: T] of a liquid, in degrees Fahrenheit, [MATH: t] minutes after it starts cooling is given by

[MATH: T(t) = 80 - 1.75t.]
What will the temperature be after [MATH: 24] minutes?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We are told that the temperature is given by the function

[MATH: T(t) = 80 - 1.75t,]
where [MATH: t] represents the number of minutes after cooling starts.

We substitute [MATH: t = 24] into the temperature function:

[MATH: T(24)|= 80 − 1.75(24); = 80 − 42; = 38.]

Thus, the temperature will be [MATH: 38^\circ\mathrm{F}] after [MATH: 24] minutes.

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Interpreting Statements Given in Function Notation

Content:
Suppose that the daily profit [MATH: P,] in dollars, of a particular restaurant can be represented by the function

Content:
[MATH: P(n) = 20n - 150,]
where [MATH: n] is the number of guests visiting the restaurant that day.

Content:
Now, suppose we want to interpret the following statement in this context:

Content:
[MATH: P(20) = 250]

Content:
To interpret this statement, we begin by breaking it down:

Content:
- the input [MATH: n=20] represents the number of visitors, while
- the output [MATH: P = 250] is the corresponding profit.

Content:
Therefore, the statement [MATH: P({\color{blue}20}) = {\color{red}250}] can be interpreted as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] When [MATH: \color{blue}20] visitors come to the restaurant, the restaurant earns a [MATH: \color{red}\[math]250] profit.

---

Item 6 — Example: Interpreting Function Notation in an Applied Context

Example Prompt:
The number of people living in Pasadena, California, can be modeled by the function
[MATH: N(t) = 1\,750t + 138\,000,]
where [MATH: t] is the number of years since the year [MATH: 2011.] What does the statement [MATH: N(3) > N(2)] mean in this context?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we interpret [MATH: N(3)] and [MATH: N(2)] separately:

- [MATH: N(3)] represents the number of people living in Pasadena [MATH: 3] years after [MATH: 2011,] that is, in [MATH: 2014.]
- [MATH: N(2)] represents the number of people living in Pasadena [MATH: 2] years after [MATH: 2011,] that is, in [MATH: 2013.]

Therefore, the statement [MATH: N(3) > N(2)] means the following:

[MATH: \qquad] "More people lived in Pasadena in [MATH: 2014] compared to [MATH: 2013.]"

---

Item 9 — Tutorial: Interpreting Parts of a Function

Content:
Recall that the daily profit [MATH: P] of a restaurant, in dollars, can be represented by the function

Content:
[MATH: P(n) = 20n - 150,]
where [MATH: n] is the number of visitors to the restaurant that day.

Content:
We can interpret the various parts of the function [MATH: P(n)] as follows:

Content:
- The constant [MATH: -150] is the amount of profit the restaurant earns when [MATH: 0] visitors come to the restaurant. In other words, the restaurant loses [MATH: \[math]150] if no visitors come.
- The coefficient [MATH: 20] is the amount of additional profit that the restaurant earns for each visitor that comes to the restaurant.

---

Item 10 — Example: Interpreting Parts of a Function in an Applied Context

Example Prompt:
The number of hours per year that people in a particular country spent on social media can be modeled by the function
[MATH: h(x)= 12x+305,]
where [MATH: x] is the number of years since the year [MATH: 2000.] What does the constant [MATH: 305] mean in this context?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Notice that by substituting [MATH: x=0] into our function, we get
[MATH: h(0) = 12 \cdot 0 + 305 = 305.]

The value [MATH: x=0] corresponds to the year [MATH: 2000.] So in [MATH: 2000,] the people in this country spent [MATH: 305] hours per year on social media.

Therefore, the constant term [MATH: 305] represents the number of hours per year that people in this country spent on social media in [MATH: 2000.]
